counterexample:
Take n = 2, (x1, x2) = (1, 2), p = -1, q = 0. These satisfy every hypothesis of the theorem: p, q are extended reals with p < q, the x_k are real and > 0 (required since p < 0). The theorem therefore asserts M_{-1}(1,2) <= M_0(1,2), i.e. 2/(1 + 1/2) = 4/3 = 1.3333... <= sqrt(1*2) = 1.41421..., which is true but is nowhere established by the proof.

Why step 0040 fails on this instance: step 0040 claims 'It remains to resolve the inequality for p, q in R_{>=0}', i.e. that after the preceding steps the only open cases are those with both exponents real and nonnegative. Track this instance through the preceding steps:
  - Steps 0001-0029 only conclude M_infty >= M_p and M_{-infty} <= M_p; neither exponent here is +/-infty, so they say nothing.
  - Step 0031 opens the case 'p = 0 or q = 0', which this instance is in (q = 0), but steps 0033-0038 only restate the definition M_0 = G and its limit justification. No inequality of any kind is derived in that block, and the block is closed at 0040 with no {{qed|lemma}} and no conclusion. So the case is opened and abandoned.
  - The instance is not in the residual set named by 0040 either, since p = -1 is not in R_{>=0}.
Hence the pair (p,q) = (-1,0) is a concrete witness that the case split is not exhaustive: it belongs to no resolved case and to no case step 0040 says remains.

The subsequent machinery cannot absorb it. For q = 0 the function of step 0043 is phi(x) = x^{q/p} = x^{0/(-1)} = x^0 = 1, a constant. Step 0046 gives phi'(x) = (q/p) x^{q/p-1} = 0, which is neither strictly increasing nor strictly decreasing, so 0049 and 0052 both fail. Jensen at 0057 degenerates to ((1/2)(1^{-1} + 2^{-1}))^0 = 1 <= (1/2)(1^0 + 2^0) = 1, i.e. 1 <= 1, from which raising to the power 1/q = 1/0 is undefined and no comparison of M_{-1} with M_0 can be extracted. So the geometric-mean case is genuinely unproved, not merely unstated.

A second, independent witness that step 0040's residual set is too small: n = 2, (x1, x2) = (1, 2), p = -2, q = -1. Again p < q, all x_k > 0. Here M_{-2} = ((1/2)(1 + 1/4))^{-1/2} = (5/8)^{-1/2} = 1.26491..., M_{-1} = ((1/2)(1 + 1/2))^{-1} = (3/4)^{-1} = 1.33333..., so the claimed inequality holds; but both exponents are strictly negative, so this pair lies outside R_{>=0}, outside the +/-infty lemmas of 0001-0029, and outside the p = 0 or q = 0 case of 0031. Under the scope announced at 0040 it is never treated at all (and the later steps 0052 and 0059, which speak of q < 0, contradict that announced scope rather than repairing it).
reasoning_summary: Steps 0001-0029 are fine: they cite the p = +/-infty definitions/limits and the standard 'max >= M_p' and 'min <= M_p' lemmas to get the two infinite-exponent statements, and each is closed with a lemma qed. Step 0031 opens the case 'p = 0 or q = 0'; steps 0033-0038 correctly record M_0 = G with the limit justification, but derive no inequality. Step 0040 then asserts that what remains is p, q in R_{>=0}. This is the first step that definitely fails, and it fails twice over: (i) it treats the p = 0 or q = 0 case as discharged when only a definition was quoted, no comparison M_p <= M_0 <= M_q was ever proved, and the later Jensen argument degenerates there (phi = x^{q/p} is either undefined for p = 0 or constant for q = 0, giving the vacuous 1 <= 1 and an undefined exponent 1/q); and (ii) the residual set R_{>=0} omits all pairs with p < q < 0, which the proof's own later steps 0052 and 0059 then discuss, contradicting the scope just declared. Concrete witnesses (p,q) = (-1,0) and (-2,-1) with (x1,x2) = (1,2) satisfy the theorem's hypotheses yet fall in no case that any step through 0040 resolves. Further downstream problems exist but are not needed for the verdict: the convexity/concavity claims at 0049/0052 are justified by the sign of q alone, whereas x^{q/p} is strictly convex iff q/p > 1 or q/p < 0 and strictly concave iff 0 < q/p < 1 (the conclusions happen to survive under p < q but the stated criterion is not the right one), and step 0061 proves only the 'x_1 = ... = x_n' half of the equality characterisation, never addressing the theorem's second equality clause (q < 0 with some x_k = 0).
